label.trigger: NumberUtils.createNumber gets a decimal string without a type suffix that carries more significant digits than a float keeps, but whose nearest double happens to be exactly representable as a float, e.g. "0.100000001490116121".
label.expected_impact: The Float shortcut accepts the input because the double parse and the float parse round to the same binary value, so a Float is returned whose decimal form (0.1 for the example) no longer matches the text. The trailing digits are dropped silently instead of falling through to the Double/BigDecimal branch that keeps the exact value, so printing, re-serialising or converting the result to BigDecimal yields different data than the caller supplied.

context_locations.note: The Double branch right below only returns a Double when it equals the exact BigDecimal of the text; the Float shortcut above skips any comparable exactness test, which shows the intended rule.

anchors.start: * If a type specifier is not found, it will check for a decimal point

context_locations.note: The method documentation promises to move on to wider types, ending at BigDecimal, which only makes sense if a narrower type is chosen when it keeps the value.

known_counterevidence.note: For the affected inputs the returned Float widens to the same double that Double.valueOf would give, so callers that only use doubleValue() see no change; the loss appears through toString, floatValue-based storage or BigDecimal conversion.
The second half of the condition, matching shortest decimal forms of the float and the double, is sound and stays; only the binary-equality alternative lets imprecise Floats through.

label.fix_summary: Drop the alternative that accepts a Float when the double rounds to the same binary value, and return a Float only if its shortest decimal text equals the double's; other inputs continue to the Double branch, which hands back a BigDecimal when the double is not exact.

check.summary: A main program compiled against src/main/java feeds five decimal strings to NumberUtils.createNumber and compares the BigDecimal of each result's toString with the BigDecimal of its input; any mismatch is a violation.
check.failure_signature: CHECK-VIOLATION: createNumber changed the value of \d+ decimal input

verification.summary: verify --run-checks with OpenJDK 21: the check program compiles with the whole src/main/java on the fix parent and on the fix commit. On before createNumber("0.100000001490116121") returns Float 0.1 and the program exits 1 with CHECK-VIOLATION; on after it returns BigDecimal 0.100000001490116121 and the four short inputs keep their Float/Double results (exit 0). The upstream JUnit test added by the fix was not run; the check is an independent main program.
